title: Sylvester-Gallai Theorem via Kelly's Proof
description: Formalizes the Sylvester-Gallai theorem using Kelly's elegant extremal proof (1948). Any finite set of ≥3 non-collinear points has a line through exactly 2 points. The proof uses a minimum-distance argument; the key geometric inequality is axiomatized.

overview.historicalContext: J.J. Sylvester posed the problem in 1893, Gallai proved it in 1944, and L.M. Kelly gave the beautiful extremal proof in 1948. Kelly's proof chooses the nearest point-line pair and derives a contradiction if the line has ≥3 points, using only the triangle inequality and elementary coordinate geometry.
overview.problemStatement: For any finite set of $\geq 3$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, not all on one line, prove there exists a line through exactly 2 of the points.
overview.text: Formalizes Sylvester-Gallai via Kelly's elegant minimum-distance proof.
overview.proofStrategy: Kelly's proof: (1) Among all pairs (point $p$, line $\ell$ through $\geq 2$ points) with $p \notin \ell$, choose the pair minimizing $d(p, \ell)$. (2) If $\ell$ has $\geq 3$ points, coordinate geometry shows we can find a strictly closer pair. (3) Contradiction, so $\ell$ has exactly 2 points.
keyInsights: Kelly's proof is purely extremal: minimize distance, then show ≥3 points leads to contradiction
The coordinate calculation: d(a, line(p,c)) = h(γ-α)/√(h²+γ²) < h because α(α-2γ) ≤ 0 < h²
The key lemma is a candidate for Aristotle (routine coordinate inequality after setup)
